track.title: Algebra 1
track.summary: A first algebra path focused on unknowns, relationships, expressions, equations, and functions.

orientationEssays.title: What is Algebra 1?
orientationEssays.plainLanguageSummary: Algebra is a language for representing unknown quantities and relationships. It turns a hidden value into something you can name, reason about, and solve.
orientationEssays.historicalOrigin: Algebra grew from practical problems in trade, inheritance, surveying, astronomy, and engineering. Mathematical traditions across many cultures shaped it, including Arabic work on al-jabr, restoration or completion.
orientationEssays.socialImportance: Modern life is full of hidden variables: prices, rates, loans, growth, risk, motion, and code. Algebra helps people represent those hidden pieces instead of guessing.
orientationEssays.whyLearnersCare: When algebra clicks, many problems stop feeling like isolated tricks. You gain a reusable way to describe patterns, compare options, and solve for missing information.
commonObjections: Learners often ask why letters appear in math when numbers seem more concrete.
Some learners think algebra is only useful for tests, not for daily decisions.
deeperPaths: Study how algebra connects to coordinate graphs and linear functions.
Explore how symbolic algebra supports programming, physics, economics, and statistics.

orientationEssays.title: Why simplify expressions?
orientationEssays.plainLanguageSummary: Simplifying expressions is the habit of saying the same relationship in a cleaner form. You are not changing the meaning, only removing clutter.
orientationEssays.historicalOrigin: As algebra notation became more compact, mathematicians needed reliable rules for rewriting expressions without changing their value. Combining like terms is one of those basic rules.
orientationEssays.socialImportance: Clear symbolic expressions help engineers, analysts, programmers, and scientists avoid mistakes when a relationship has many moving parts.
orientationEssays.whyLearnersCare: Simplifying makes later equation solving easier. If you can turn a messy expression into a cleaner one, you can see the actual structure of the problem.
commonObjections: It can feel like busywork until learners see that simplification preserves meaning.
Learners often wonder why unlike terms cannot be combined.
deeperPaths: Connect simplification to the distributive property and factoring.
Use expression trees to see how software represents algebra.
sourceNotes: Seeded as a concept-level orientation essay for the first Algebra 1 vertical slice.

concepts.title: Parts of an Algebraic Expression
concepts.summary: Variables, coefficients, constants, and like terms are the vocabulary needed to simplify expressions.
objectives: Identify variables, coefficients, constants, and like terms in a linear expression.

hints: Add the coefficients and keep the variable the same.

feedback.correct: Correct. Four y terms plus seven y terms makes eleven y terms.
feedback.incorrect: When terms have the same variable and exponent, add only the coefficients.

evidenceRequired: Correctly combines like terms without changing exponents.

hints: Subtract the coefficients of the like terms.

feedback.incorrect: Do not change the exponent when combining like terms.

misconceptions.description: Learner adds exponents when combining like terms, such as treating 3x + 2x as 5x^2.

remediation.message: Return to concrete groups: three x groups plus two x groups equals five x groups.

concepts.title: Simplifying Algebraic Expressions
concepts.summary: Simplify expressions by distributing and combining like terms.
objectives: Use the distributive property and like terms to simplify a linear algebraic expression.

hints: First multiply 5 by each term inside the parentheses.

feedback.correct: Correct. You distributed first, then combined like terms.
feedback.incorrect: Check whether every term inside the parentheses was multiplied by 5.

hints: Distribute the 3, then subtract one x term.

feedback.incorrect: After distributing, remember to combine 6x and -x.

misconceptions.description: Learner multiplies only the variable term and forgets to distribute to the constant.

remediation.message: Use arrows from the outside factor to every term inside the parentheses.
